title: Kalshi court losses pile up as judges refuse to block state gambling laws
gist: Kalshi lost bids in the Ninth Circuit (Nevada, en banc rehearing denied with no judge in favor) and the Second Circuit (New York, Connecticut, and Coinbase) to block state gambling laws, and was sued by Arkansas after Utah filed criminal charges. Its only appellate win is the Third Circuit's New Jersey ruling that its sports contracts are CFTC-regulated swaps. With the circuits split and 39 states backing New Jersey's Supreme Court petition, the issue is heading to the Supreme Court, while the Trump administration's CFTC sues states on prediction markets' behalf.

themes.theme: Circuit split on prediction markets as swaps

insights.claim: The Ninth Circuit unanimously ruled in August 2026 that Kalshi sports bets are not swaps and Nevada can regulate them under state gambling law, and none of its 29 judges supported Kalshi's petition for en banc rehearing.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Not a single judge supporting rehearing signals a firm legal setback for Kalshi's sports contracts, its key growth product, in Western states.
insights.quote: “The full court has been advised of the petition for rehearing en banc and no judge has requested a vote on whether to rehear the matter en banc,”
insights.locator: Kalshi sought to overturn the judges’ panel

insights.claim: The Second Circuit upheld lower-court denials of preliminary injunctions that Kalshi sought against New York and Connecticut gambling laws, and also refused to overturn Coinbase's loss against Connecticut on the same issues.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Coinbase's prediction market ambitions face the same state-law exposure as Kalshi's.

insights.claim: The Sixth Circuit unanimously ruled in September 2026 that Ohio and Tennessee can enforce their gambling laws against Kalshi.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Losses in multiple circuits shrink the states where prediction markets can legally offer sports contracts.

insights.claim: Kalshi's biggest win came in April 2026 when the Third Circuit ruled its sports event contracts are swaps on a CFTC-licensed designated contract market, giving the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction and blocking New Jersey regulation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The Third Circuit ruling conflicts with the others, creating a circuit split that makes Supreme Court review likely.
insights.quote: “Kalshi’s sports-related event contracts are swaps traded on a CFTC-licensed DCM [designated contract market], so the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction,”
insights.locator: Kalshi’s biggest win came in April

insights.claim: New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to reverse its Third Circuit loss, supported by a brief from 39 other states and the District of Columbia, suggesting the Supreme Court may ultimately decide whether states can regulate prediction markets.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A Supreme Court decision will be the deciding event for the prediction market industry's US business model.

insights.claim: Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin sued Kalshi in state court, alleging it offers unlicensed gambling to people as young as 18 (below Arkansas's 21 minimum for electronic wagering) and fails to pay taxes.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Age-limit and tax arguments give states solid grounds for enforcement and expose Kalshi to back-tax claims.
insights.quote: “Arkansas law is concerned with substance, not semantics,”

insights.claim: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown lodged criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders for violating Utah's gambling ban, after a federal judge ruled Utah can enforce its anti-gambling laws against Kalshi.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Criminal charges against founders are a sharp escalation beyond civil regulatory disputes.

insights.claim: Kalshi argues markets cannot operate when rules change at every state line, which is why Congress created a single federal regulator with nationwide rules.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Kalshi's business model depends on federal preemption, so if that argument fails it would need state-by-state licensing like sportsbooks.
insights.quote: “Markets can’t operate when the rules change at every state line, which is why Congress created a single federal regulator, with nationwide rules.
insights.locator: Kalshi said in response to Arkansas’ lawsuit

insights.claim: The CFTC, claiming sole authority over platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, has sued Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Utah, and Wisconsin over their efforts to enforce gambling laws.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Federal backing is a support for prediction markets, but it depends on politics and could change with the administration.

insights.claim: Donald Trump Jr. serves as an advisor to Kalshi in exchange for a generous equity deal, while the Trump administration sides with Kalshi in its legal fights with states.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Political ties raise conflict-of-interest questions and add policy risk if the administration changes.
